1
INTEREST OF AMICUS1
The Freedom From Religion Foundation (“FFRF”)
is the largest national association of freethinkers,
representing atheists, agnostics, and others who form
their opinions about religion based on reason, rather
than faith, tradition, or authority. Founded nationally
in 1978 as a 501(c) (3) nonprofit, FFRF has more than
40,000 members, including members in every state and
the District of Columbia. FFRF’s primary purposes are
to educate about nontheism and to preserve the cherished
constitutional principle of separation between religion and
government.
FFRF also seeks to protect equal access to the courts
for civil rights litigants in this realm. Courts must not
stray from longstanding jurisdictional principles to afford
leniency to religiously-affiliated litigants while using
the same principles to deny access to other civil rights
litigants.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Article III of the Constitution limits federal courts’
power to only adjudicate actual cases and controversies.
In this pre-enforcement challenge, Grand asks the Court
to disregard Article III limitations and issue an advisory
opinion. The Court should decline to adjudicate this case
1. No party’s counsel in this case authored this brief in whole
or in part. No party or party’s counsel contributed any money
intended to fund preparing or submitting this brief. No person,
other than amicus, its members, or its counsel contributed money
that was intended to fund preparing or submitting this brief.

2
for two reasons: Grand lacks standing and his claims are
moot.
First, Grand’s claim for prospective relief from the
zoning ordinance under the First Amendment is moot.
Grand has moved out of the City and is no longer subject
to the zoning ordinance. There is no reasonable threat that
the zoning ordinance could ever be enforced against him.
Second, Grand lacks standing to challenge the zoning
ordinance under a Free Exercise claim. In order to
demonstrate standing in a pre-enforcement challenge, a
Petitioner must establish that there is a substantial threat
of future enforcement of the law they are challenging.
Here, the zoning ordinance, by admission of both parties,
has not ever and will not ever be enforced against Grand.
Instead, Grand attempts to argue that he was chilled from
exercising his rights. However, there is no evidence that
the City ever intended to enforce the zoning ordinance
against Grand or anyone else for small, informal prayer
gatherings. The City was clear that it would enforce the
ordinance against any use of Grand’s home as a house of
worship, but Grand has avowed that he never intended
to use his home that way. He has demonstrated no intent
to engage in any conduct that would arguably violate the
ordinance. Therefore, he cannot establish standing to
challenge the ordinance.
Finally, Grand belatedly attempts to challenge
the zoning ordinance based on retrospective injuries.
However, he did not pursue these claims in his motion for
summary judgment or before the Sixth Circuit. The Court
should not allow the reintroduction of these claims at this
stage, which would require the Court to parse a very

3
muddled factual record, because Grand’s alleged injuries
are not fairly traceable to the zoning ordinance. Any past
injuries are the result of a series of miscommunications.
The Court must not disregard Article III limitations
and should dismiss this case or, alternatively, affirm the
court of appeals.
ARGUMENT
Grand’s petition for certiorari raised the spectre of a
government using a zoning ordinance to restrict citizens
from gathering in small groups to engage in religious
activity on private property. See Pet. for Cert. While
such action by the government would be constitutionally
suspect, Grand’s petition doesn’t deliver. The City
never intended to weaponize its ordinance in the way
Grand describes and the ordinance was never enforced
against Grand. His alleged injuries do not arise from
the ordinance at all, but rather, from a messy series of
miscommunications.
In order to have a justiciable case or controversy, the
case cannot be moot and the plaintiff must have standing
to sue. See DeFunis v. Odegaard, 416 U.S. 312, 316 (1974)
(“The inability of the federal judiciary ‘to review moot
cases derives from the requirement of Art. III of the
Constitution under which the exercise of judicial power
depends upon the existence of a case or controversy.’”)
(quoting Liner v. Jafco, Inc., 375 U.S. 301, 306 n.3 (1964));
DaimlerChrysler Corp. v. Cuno , 126 U.S. 1854, 1862
(2006) (“[A] core component of the case-or-controversy
requirement is that a litigant has standing to invoke the
authority of a federal court.”).

4
Mootness is a question that federal courts must answer
if they “are to function within their constitutional sphere
of authority.” N.C. v. Rice, 404 U.S. 244, 246 (1971). For
federal courts to have authority, “parties must continue
to have a ‘personal stake in the outcome’ of the lawsuit.”
Lewis v. Cont. Bank Corp. , 494 U.S. 472, 478 (1990). This
requirement “subsists through all stages of federal judicial
proceedings, trial and appellate.” Id. at 477.
Standing is a “bedrock constitutional requirement
that applies to all manners of important disputes.” Food
& Drug Admin. v. Alliance for Hippocratic Med. , 602
U.S. 367, 378 (2024). As a bedrock principle, “Article III
demands that an actual controversy persist throughout all
stages of litigation.” Hollingsworth v. Perry, 570 U.S. 693,
704 (2013); see Nat’l Org. for Women, Inc. v. Scheidler, 510
U.S. 249, 255 (1994) (“Standing remains open to review at
all stages of litigation.”). This remains true on appellate
review, where appellants must establish all Article III
standing requirements just like they had to in courts of
first instance. See Arizonans for Off. Eng. v. Arizona, 520
U.S. 43, 64 (1997).
I.  No prospective relief is available against the zoning
ordinance because the claim is moot and Grand
lacks standing.
Grand no longer lives in the City and thus the zoning
ordinance cannot be enforced against him, making his
claims for prospective relief against the ordinance moot.
Additionally, “[d]efendants, in their summary judgment
papers, have stipulated that Grand, and anyone else in the
City, can hold small, informal religious (or non-religious)
gatherings on a regular basis and such activity is not

5
subject to any of the City’s ordinances or permitting
requirements.” Dist. Ct. Am. Mem. Op. Order 14, Oct. 1,
2024. Pet. App. 39a. The City agrees that Grand can hold
the gatherings he asserts he wanted to host, or at least
he could if he still lived in University Heights.
A.  Grand mooted his own claims for prospective
relief by moving out of the City.
To avoid being dismissed for mootness, “an actual
controversy must be extant at all stages of review, not
merely at the time the complaint is filed.” Alvarez v. Smith,
558 U.S. 87, 92 (2009) (quoting Preiser v. Newkirk , 422
U.S. 395, 401 (1975). “[A] dispute solely about the meaning
of a law, abstracted from any concrete actual or threatened
harm, falls outside the scope of the constitutional words
‘Cases’ and ‘Controversies.’” Alvarez, 558 U.S. at 93. For
a court to speak on the constitutionality of a law when it
has not established jurisdiction is “by very definition, for
a court to act ultra vires.” Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better
Env’t, 523 U.S. 83, 101 (1998).
Claims for prospective relief are moot when a
plaintiff’s changed circumstances mean that the plaintiff
is no longer subject to the government regulation at issue.
See Arizonans for Off. English , 520 U.S. at 67–72. In
Arizonans for Official English , the plaintiff was a state
employee subject to a regulation that said English was
the official language of all state government functions
and actions. Id. at 48. During the litigation, the plaintiff
voluntarily left state employment and did not allege she
planned to return. Id. Because her changed circumstances
meant that she was no longer subject to the regulation,
the claim was moot. Id. at 72.

6
Here, Grand was living in University Heights and
thus at least theoretically subject to its zoning ordinance
at the time this suit was filed. Letter of Resp’t Regarding
Pet’r’s Move Sept. 21, 2026. However, Grand moved out of
University Heights in July 2026 and does not own property
in the City. Letter Notifying Ct. of Pet’r’s Move Sept. 18,
2026. He does not allege that he has any plans to ever move
back to University Heights. Id. The zoning ordinance only
applies to property within the City. Therefore, Grand is
no longer subject to the zoning ordinance and his claims
for prospective relief are moot.
Parties have an ongoing duty to timely notify the
courts of changed circumstances that could affect
ongoing litigation. In Board of License Commissioners
of Town of Tiverton v. Pastore , this Court held that
because the petitioner-business went out of business
during the litigation, the case was moot. See 469 U.S. 238,
239–40 (1985). The Court learned of this after it issued
a writ of certiorari, considered briefs on the merits, and
commenced oral argument. Id. at 239. Nevertheless,
this Court reminded counsel that there is a “continuing
duty to inform the Court of any development which may
conceivably affect the outcome of the litigation.” Id.
at 240. “When a development after this Court grants
certiorari . . . could have the effect of depriving the Court
of jurisdiction due to the absence of a continuing case . . .
that development should be called to the attention of the
Court without delay .” Id.
In this case, the City alleges Grand listed his home
in University Heights for sale four days after filing his
reply brief in support of his petition for certiorari. The
deed to the University Heights home was transferred

7
on July 9, 2026, seventy-one days before Grand filed
the letter notifying the Court that he had moved out of
the City. The City states it discovered these facts and
contacted Grand and his counsel about his move just two
days before Grand’s counsel filed the Letter of Notification
to this Court. Letter of Resp’t’s Regarding Pet’r’s Move
Sept. 21, 2026. This timing is, at the very least, suspicious.
Arguably Grand’s counsel failed in its duty to notify the
Court of Grand’s changed circumstances, which have
obvious implications for his standing to sue.
A potential failure to properly notify the Court
of circumstances that moot this case is especially
problematic here, given how Alliance Defending Freedom,
which serves as counsel to Grand, has litigated other
free exercise challenges. Alliance Defending Freedom
previously represented the plaintiffs in Telescope Media
Group v. Lucero, 936 F .3d 740 (8th Cir. 2019). The
plaintiffs in that case alleged that they intended to put a
discriminatory statement on a film business website and
that they wanted to expand their business to wedding
videography. They sought to enter this market because
they were “deeply troubled” by the United States Supreme
Court’s decision in Obergefell v. Hodges , 576 U.S. 644
(2015). After a favorable ruling before the Eighth Circuit
and the subsequent issuance of a preliminary injunction
by the district court, Telescope Media discontinued its
pursuit of a wedding videography business. See Telescope
Media Grp. v. Lucero, No. 16-cv-4094, 2021 WL 2525412,
at *1 (available online at https://bit.ly/3dv7gUd).2 After
2. The plaintiffs asserted, in part, that this was because of
live-event restrictions associated with the coronavirus pandemic.
2021 WL 2525412, at *1  However, they acknowledged in the fall of
2020 that they had no intent to reenter the wedding business. Id.

8
receiving discovery requests from the state, Telescope
Media sought to dismiss its case. 2021 WL 2525412, at
*2. It appeared that Telescope Media had not seriously
entered into the wedding videography business. The
district court correctly identified that Telescope’s case
was likely a sham. The district court said it was “a smoke
and mirrors case or controversy from the beginning,
likely conjured up by Plaintiffs to establish binding First
Amendment precedent rather than to allow them to craft
wedding videos, of which they have made exactly two.”
Id. at *3.
This Court has not escaped from being drawn into
jurisdictionally dubious cases in recent years, like in
Kennedy v. Bremerton , where Joseph Kennedy moved
2,800 miles from the Washington school district at issue in
his case to live in Florida, where he established himself as
a resident. Br. for Freedom From Religion Foundation, et
al. as Amici Curiae in Support of Resp’t at 6–7, Kennedy
v. Bremerton Sch. Dist ., 597 U.S. 507 (2022) (No. 21-418).
This Court chose to remain silent on Kenney’s move and
adjudicated his case as if there were still a live controversy.
After Kennedy prevailed, he created a media spectacle by
returning to Bremerton School District for only a single
football game before resigning as coach and returning
to Florida. See Paradise Afshar, Football Coach who
Won Supreme Court Case for Right to Pray on the Field
Resigns After One Game , CNN (Sept. 6, 2023) https://
tinyurl.com/4j75kbuu . Kennedy’s alleged injuries were
not redressed by this Court’s decision. His case was moot
before it was decided.
Similar justiciability and redressability concerns
arose in 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis , where the plaintiff

9
website designer had never designed wedding websites in
the first place. See 600 U.S. 570, 624 (2023). The designer
merely claimed that she wanted to get into that business.
Id. Likewise, in Chiles v. Salazar , this Court ruled that
regulations preventing therapists from engaging in
conversion therapy were restrictions on speech. See 607
U.S. 627 (2026). However, the plaintiff therapist, Chiles,
stated that she never intended to violate the conversion
therapy ban or practice conversion therapy. See Br. for
Freedom From Religion Found. as Amicus Curiae in
Support of Resp’ts, Chiles v. Salazar, 607 U.S. 627 (2026)
(No. 24-539). Like in Kennedy, there was no injury in these
cases that the Court’s opinion could actually redress.
If the Court does not adhere to its precedent on
mootness, this case is likely to yield a similar result: a
ruling that will not truly redress any alleged injuries .
Grand himself may not have been aware that his move
to a new town would create a jurisdictional problem for
this Court. His attorneys, however, should have known of
the mootness issue and of their duty to notify the Court
of Grand’s move as soon as it arose. They failed to do so.
In fact, Grand’s opening brief, filed after his move out
of University Heights, alleges that he lost “292 weeks’
worth” of his small prayer gatherings—the number of
weeks between January 2021 and its filing—despite Grand
having ceased being a resident of University Heights for
at least ten of those weeks. Pet. Br. 16. It is apparent that
the ultimate prize in this case is not to ensure that Grand
can host small, informal prayer gatherings at a home in
University Heights. Instead, it appears this case is now a
“smoke and mirrors” challenge meant to advance a policy
agenda, but afford no actual relief to the petitioner. This
Court’s jurisdictional requirements are in place in part

10
to ensure that the Court cannot be manipulated in this
manner.
B.  Grand lacks Article III standing to seek
prospective relief against the zoning ordinance
under the Free Exercise Clause because both
parties agree that the permit requirement does
not apply to Grand’s intended gatherings.
To establish standing, a plaintiff must demonstrate:
(i) that she has suffered or will likely suffer an injury in
fact, (ii) that the injury likely was caused or will be caused
by the defendant, and (iii) that the injury likely would be
redressed by the requested judicial relief. Alliance for
Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 380. For pre-enforcement
cases, a plaintiff satisfies the injury-in-fact requirement
when he (1) alleges he intends to engage in conduct that
arguably has a constitutional interest, (2) that the intended
future conduct is arguably proscribed by the challenged
statute, and (3) that the threat of future enforcement is
substantial. Susan B. Anthony List v. Driehaus, 573 U.S.
149, 159 (2014).
In his complaint, Grand sought orders and injunctions
proscribing future action by the City to enforce the
zoning ordinance. JA 94–96. Though his complaint did
mention damages for retrospective relief, his motion for
summary judgement argued only the prospective claims
and made no mention of damages at all. See D. Ct. Dkt.
81. At the Sixth Circuit, Grand also focused entirely on
his prospective challenge to the zoning ordinance. C.A.
Reply Br. 1. The zoning ordinance has not been enforced
against Grand. He failed to pursue his damages claims at
summary judgement and before the Sixth Circuit. Thus,

11
Grand must meet the pre-enforcement injury-in-fact
standard to establish standing. He has failed to do so.
Despite Grand’s insistence that he was subject to a
“credible threat of enforcement,” he does not establish
that his proposed informal prayer gatherings arguably
violate the ordinance. In fact, he and the City agree that
this kind of small, informal gathering would not require
a permit. Pet. Opening Br. 31.
This Court has found that when the statute at
issue would no longer be applicable to the intended
conduct asserted by petitioners, there is not a justiciable
controversy. See, e.g., Golden v. Zwickler , 394 U.S. 103,
109 (1969). In Golden, the plaintiff challenged a leafleting
ordinance because he wanted to leaflet against a specific
candidate. Id. at 104–05. That candidate was no longer
running for office and was unlikely to run in the immediate
future. Id. at 106. Since the statute only applied to leaflets
in election campaigns and there was no real or immediate
prospect of a campaign by the candidate, this Court said
it was “wholly conjectural that another occasion might
arise when [the plaintiff] might be prosecuted.” Id. at 109.
Here, the City believed that Grand wanted to have
huge gatherings of people at his home, on a weekly basis.
The City has maintained that large gatherings of that
kind would need a special use permit. However, as it
became clear that Grand had intended only to host a small
gathering of people, the City acquiesced that such a small
gathering was “not [its] business.” JA 325. The ordinance
is not applicable to the conduct Grand asserts he wanted
to engage in, hosting small prayer gatherings. Thus, like
Golden, this “injury” is “wholly conjectural.”

12
Grand alleges that First Choice Women’s Resource
Centers, Inc. v. Davenport, 608 U.S. 174 (2026), establishes
that an injury in fact arises and remains as long as “a
demand” is made and remains outstanding. Pet. Opening
Br. 30. That may be true when, unlike here, certain
conditions are met. In contrast to the present case, in First
Choice the Attorney General issued a subpoena to First
Choice for their donor records. See id.  at 178–80. There
was no question that the subpoena, whether valid or not,
was being applied against the organization.
That is the fundamental flaw in Grand’s injury-in-fact
argument. First Choice ’s facts would only be analogous
here if the Planning Commission had determined that
Grand needed a permit to invite a small group of people to
his home to pray and had then filed an enforcement action
against him. Only then would the facts have been clear that
the zoning ordinance was being applied against Grand like
the subpoena was against First Choice. A subpoena is a
legally enforceable document. There is no such analogous
legal document here. In fact, at this point, the City’s clear
stance is that Grand did not need to apply for a permit to
host these gatherings. Def.’s Br. in Opp’n to Pl.’s Mot. for
Summ. J. at 2419–20. Further, the ordinance cannot be
applied against Grand’s prayer gatherings in the future
as he no longer lives in University Heights.
The agreement by both parties that Grand would
not need a permit to host the gatherings he intended to
host is destructive to all of his arguments that the Court
has jurisdiction. In all cases cited by Grand regarding
injury in fact where the plaintiff had standing, the
plaintiff expressly stated an intent to engage in, or had
engaged in, conduct that was arguably proscribed by the

13
statute. See, e.g., Va. v. Am. Booksellers Ass’n, Inc. , 484
U.S. 383, 390–91 (1988) (“The booksellers introduced
as exhibits a total of 16 books that they believed were
examples of books the amended statute covered, and
testified that the law might apply to as much as one half
of their inventory.”); Steffel v. Thompson , 415 U.S. 452,
456 (1974) (“Petitioner alleged in his complaint that . . .
he desired to return to the shopping center to distribute
handbills. . . .”); Bantam Books, Inc. v. Sullivan , 372
U.S. 58, 63 (1963) (“Silverstein had received at least 35
such notices [that his book was subject to an obscenity
law]”); City of Lakewood v. Plain Dealer Publ’g Co. , 486
U.S. 750, 753 (1988) (“the city denied the Plain Dealer
Publishing Company (Newspaper) permission to place
its coin-operated newspaper dispensing devices on city
sidewalks.”); Watchtower Bible & Tract Society of N.Y.,
Inc. v. Vill. of Stratton , 536 U.S. 150, 153–54, 161 (2002)
(“[Jehovah’s Witnesses] brought this action . . . seeking
an injunction against the enforcement of . . . Ordinance
No. 1998–5 regulating uninvited peddling and solicitation
on private property in the Village.”); Freedman v. Md. ,
380 U.S. 51, 52 (1965) (Appellant sought to challenge
the constitutionality of the Maryland . . . statute . . . and
exhibited the film . . . without first submitting the picture
to the State Board of Censors as required by s 2 thereof.”);
Shuttlesworth v. City of Birmingham , 394 U.S. 147, 148
(1969) (The petitioner stands convicted for violating an
ordinance of Birmingham, Alabama, making it an offense
to participate in any ‘parade or procession or other public
demonstration’ without first obtaining a permit from the
City Commission.”); SBA List, 573 U.S. at 162 (“Both SBA
and COAST have alleged an intent to ‘[m]ake’ statements
‘concerning the voting record of a candidate or public
official,’ § 3517.21(B)(9). . . .”).

14
Grand claims that he never intended to host the type
of large, weekly gatherings that would have arguably
qualified as a house of worship under the zoning ordinance.
All parties agree Grand would not need a permit for his
intended gatherings. Pet’r’s Opening Br. 31; Pet. App.
38a–39a. The City did not enforce the zoning ordinance
against him and Grand withdrew his application for a
permit. The zoning ordinance does not arguably proscribe
his intended gatherings and therefore there is no threat
that the ordinance would be enforced against him, even
if he still resided in the City. Thus, Grand does not have
standing to challenge the ordinance.
II.  None of the retrospective claims that Grand now
raises give him standing to challenge the zoning
ordinance under the Free Exercise Clause.
This case is a prime example of the classic maxim “bad
facts make bad law.” In his opening brief Grand points
to alleged injuries that he hopes will breathe life into a
previously unpursued claim for retrospective relief. Pet’r’s
Opening Br. 30–33. For example, he now points to the $400
in fees he paid for his permit application, the three-hour
“public spectacle of hostility and antisemitism” of the
Planning Commission meeting, alleged “City-directed
surveillance,” and alleged retaliation. Pet. Opening Br.
31–33. But those claims do not run against the zoning
ordinance, and they do not arise from the Free Exercise
Clause. Rather than attempting to untangle one of the
messiest factual records this Court has been handed in
recent memory, the Court should simply decline to expand
Grand’s claims to include retrospective relief, and chalk up
his alleged past harms to what they are: the unfortunate
results of a series of misunderstandings.

15
The factual record in this case is a quagmire. In
2021, Grand emailed an invitation to around twelve of
his neighbors. His intentions with this communication
are disputed. Grand claims he was inviting a small group
to what he called a “shul” to pray together on a weekly
basis. Pet. App. 2a. But his invitation also described the
event as “the inauguration of the Shomayah Tefillah
Beis Hakeneset,” meaning “House of Assembly,” and
he encouraged his neighbors to “spread the word to
whomever you feel might be interested in coming”
and “bring someone with you.” J.A.344–45. One of his
neighbors then shared Grand’s invitation in a much larger
“Groveland Chat” WhatsApp group. J.A. 290.
A member of the “Groveland Chat” group then sent
Grand’s email to the Mayor, stating that someone was
“opening a synagogue in their house.” J.A. 193. The
Mayor, having recently witnessed 120–130 people meeting
in the basement of a house for another event referred to
as a “shul,” 3 forwarded Grand’s email to the City’s Law
Director who sent a cease-and-desist letter to Grand. Pet.
App. 25a. The cease-and-desist letter was directed toward
the use of Grand’s home as a place of religious assembly.
J.A. 198–200. Grand and the Mayor also spoke on the
phone where the Mayor told Grand he could not use his
home as a house of worship without a special-use permit.
Pet. App. 27a. Grand told the Mayor he only wanted to
host a small, informal prayer group, Pet. App. 3a. The
Mayor interpreted Grand’s email as an invitation to the
community to have a large group event, equivalent to a
3. Pet. App. 26a; Brennan Dep. 55:11–14; Compl. City of Univ.
Heights v. Univ. Realty USA, LLC, et al. , CV 21 948437, Cuyahoga
Cnty. Ct., Filed June 7, 2021, https://tinyurl.com/5n8mre5x .

16
house of worship, and felt that Grand’s characterizations
to the contrary on the phone were not credible, given the
content of the invitation. J.A. 320–325. Grand claims that
he did not know that his email had been sent in the large
WhatsApp chat, and it is unclear whether the Mayor was
under the impression that Grand himself had sent the
invitation to that chat. Pet. Opening Br. 7.
After the cease-and-desist letter and his subsequent
miscommunications with the Mayor over the phone, Grand
believed he needed to, and did, file a special use permit
application to host his small group prayer. Pet. App. 28a.
He also reached out to his neighbors to cancel his original
invitation. Id. At the Planning Commission meeting for
Grand’s application, Grand stated his intention to host a
small, informal prayer group. Pet. App. 29a. The meeting
ended without resolution on his application in order to get
more information about his plans. Id. at 30a. After the
meeting, many Planning Commission members expressed
to each other their doubts that Grand needed a special use
permit to host 10 or so friends. Id. at 30a–32a. Ultimately,
hours before the second meeting, Grand withdrew his
application, stating, “I do not wish to operate a house of
worship as is defined under the zoning ordinance.” Id.
at 33a. The meeting was held anyway, during which the
Mayor stated that he hoped the withdrawal was not due
to Grand now believing that meeting to “conduct activities
consistent with those in a house of assembly does not
require a special-use permit” and “there is no permission
granted here to operate . . . a house of assembly.” Id. at
33a–34a. No decision was made about Grand’s stated
intent to host only a small, informal group prayer.

17
To establish standing, an injury must be “fairly
traceable” to the challenged action. Clapper v. Amnesty
Int’l USA , 568 U.S. 398, 409 (2013). None of Grand’s
alleged retrospective injuries are fairly traceable to
enforcement of the zoning ordinance such that Grand
would have standing to challenge the ordinance under
the Free Exercise Clause. The zoning ordinance was not
enforced against Grand and facially does not apply to the
type of meeting that Grand now claims he hoped to have.
Grand’s own actions and statements make it clear that
he eventually realized that the ordinance did not apply to
small private gatherings. When he withdrew his permit
application he stated that he “did not need to seek a permit
for a small prayer group,” Pet. Br. 15, because he “d[id]
not wish to operate a house of worship as is defined under
the zoning ordinance. . . .” J.A.138. Any injuries suffered
by Grand cannot be fairly traced to the zoning ordinance
itself.
In sum, Grand has mooted his own claims for
prospective relief by moving out of University Heights. He
does not have standing to assert claims against the zoning
ordinance because all parties agree that he would not need
a permit to host these small gatherings, even if he still
lived in the City. He did not pursue any claim for damages
or other retrospective relief at summary judgement or
before the Sixth Circuit and any such injuries are not
“fairly traceable” to the City’s zoning ordinance.

18
CONCLUSION
This Court should dismiss this case for lack of
jurisdiction. Alternatively, the Court should affirm the
court of appeals.
